header.tag_why: Ines's doubt turned to "that's my number, not yours" when Wen built the business case from her own statements and costs, and the deal went to paperwork after that.

messaging_changes.current_line: Every payout reconciles automatically to its transactions and your ERP.
messaging_changes.change: For finance buyers, lead the first call with this, in their words: "Know where your money is. Every deposit matched to its transactions and your ERP, so month-end isn't a week of archaeology." Use it ahead of M1 and M2 for distributors and other non-developer, non-global buyers.
messaging_changes.why: Ines stopped the demo on payout reconciliation after the opening deck got silence, and her own phrases ("where my money is", "a week of archaeology") describe the problem more sharply than our line does.

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: Send us one month of your statements and we'll show you your own hours and dollars: what matching deposits by hand costs you at your rates, and what you'd get back. Use for finance decision-makers evaluating a switch from a bank-bundled processor.
messaging_changes.why: Ines moved from doubt to "that's my number, not yours" when the case was built from her own statements, and nothing in the interview suggests the independent study mattered.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: Do not open with this on first calls to finance leaders at regional, non-developer businesses (e.g., a distributor with a small IT team and no build plans). Keep it for global or developer-led buyers. Retire "infrastructure" from CFO-facing copy; use "deposits" and "month-end" instead.
messaging_changes.why: The standard opener got silence from a regional distributor, and nobody on the buyer side ever said "infrastructure" or even "payments"; they said "the deposits" and "the processor".

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For buyers leaving a bank-bundled incumbent: "You get a named contact who knows your business and answers your actual problem, not a rate quote." Name the people, not the tiers.
messaging_changes.why: The incumbent answered a business-problem call with "we can take a look at your rates", and after that Ines asked whether she'd get a named contact, which suggests service continuity mattered to her.

trigger.insight: The inbound said portal, but the buying event was a new CFO whose first close took nine days. Dana's account of the portal is inconsistent: she first says they were building one, then that Paul's team builds nothing and the portal is an off-the-shelf plugin. Reconciliation was only "a chunk" of the nine days, and we never learned what else slowed the close.
trigger.messaging: Stop treating web-ordering inbounds as a checkout deal; qualify for a new finance leader and a painful close, and open with the manual deposit-matching problem.

decider.insight: Paul's own words and the signature back up Dana's read that Ines decided. The costly part was that our first proposal reached her only as a forward from the IT contact and died on page one for three weeks. That detail comes secondhand, and Dana's "lost a month" doesn't line up neatly with learning about the CFO around call three.
decider.messaging: Write proposals so page one states the finance outcome in the CFO's terms, since the IT champion will forward it and the decider may read nothing else.

competitor.insight: We don't know what Fiserv pitched, so there's no competitive intel here. What we do know is that the incumbent answered a business-problem call with a price reply, and her bank rep had changed without her knowing who the new one was. Dana said her questions changed "not much" and then described a new one, so the named-contact ask was a real shift toward service continuity and Dana undersold it.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-bundled incumbents, don't lead with price or rates; say who the named people are and that they answer the customer's actual problem, rather than the generic tiered support in M5.

message.insight: M1 and M2 got silence from a regional distributor with a four-person IT team and no build plans. Ines stopped Wen mid-demo on M9, then asked to see it with her data, which shows the reconciliation story works once a finance person hears it. We pitched it as one feature in the deck, not as the lead.
message.messaging: For finance buyers, lead with M9 (every payout tied to its transactions and your ERP) and drop M1 and M2 from the first call unless the customer is global or building.

decided.insight: The deal went from "dead" (Dana's 20 percent, her own estimate) to paperwork because we modeled hours and write-offs from her own statements and cost rates, not from a generic ROI claim. Dana can't recall the exact figure and gives the 60 hours as "something like", so the proof worked but the team can't reproduce it. Nothing in the call suggests the independent study behind M6 mattered.
decided.messaging: Rework M6 around a customer-data offer, "send us one month of statements and we'll show your own hours and dollars," ahead of any generic ROI study.

gaps.insight: We had no distributor reference, and she signed anyway, so the gap didn't block the deal, though she raised it twice. The 14-branch counter question was answered only with a slide and never demoed, so M3 is unproven here. We don't know whether the in-store business is in scope, or whether "let it go" means satisfied or deferred.
gaps.messaging: Build a wholesale or distributor reference and a demo of counter card readers landing in the same reconciliation report before using M3 or M8 with this buyer type.

language.insight: Her problem is where the money went and how long it takes to close, expressed as deposits and month-end, not payments or infrastructure. The CFO and IT director even use different vocabulary for the same system. Her ownership of the number is itself the buying signal.
language.messaging: Rewrite finance-facing copy around "know where your money is" and "deposits matched at month-end," and retire "infrastructure" from CFO-facing material.

gaps.question: What did Fiserv or the bank actually offer or show, and why did Ines decide to move rather than stay?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines (or Paul) in a customer win interview what the bank proposed, what made switching worth it, and what the new bank-rep situation was.

gaps.question: What was the exact ROI figure and the hours, and how were they calculated?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen for the model and statements analysis so we can template it; Dana only remembers 'something like 60 hours' and 'low six figures'.

gaps.question: Is the 14-branch counter business in the signed scope, and did Ines need a demo that never happened?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana and Wen whether in-store readers are in the contract, and ask Ines whether the slide was enough.

gaps.question: When did the CFO actually surface, and how long was the real delay (three weeks stalled, a month lost, third call)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana for the dated timeline of calls and proposals from the CRM.

gaps.question: What else besides manual matching drove the nine-day close?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines or the controller what else slowed the close and whether we addressed it.

close.rep_takeaway: Dana, you found the real buyer on call three; next time ask on call one who owns month-end and send the proposal so the CFO can read the problem on page one. Your best move was having Wen run her own statements, so make that the default, and write the figures down so we can reuse them.
